content: Renewable energy harnesses naturally replenishing resources to generate power with minimal environmental impact compared to fossil fuels. Solar energy captures sunlight through photovoltaic cells that convert photons directly to electricity using semiconductor materials exhibiting the photoelectric effect. When photons strike these materials, they dislodge electrons, creating electric current. Solar thermal systems alternatively concentrate sunlight to heat fluids that drive turbines. Wind energy converts kinetic energy from moving air into electricity using turbines where aerodynamic blades transfer wind force to a generator. Power output follows the formula P = Â½ÏAvÂ³, where Ï is air density, A is swept area, and v is wind velocityâthe cubic relationship with velocity making wind speed crucial for efficiency. Hydropower utilizes flowing water's energy through turbines, either in run-of-river systems using natural flow or in dammed reservoirs that store potential energy for controlled release. Biomass energy derives from organic materials (plant matter, agricultural waste, dedicated energy crops) through direct combustion, gasification, or conversion to liquid biofuels like ethanol and biodiesel. Geothermal energy taps Earth's internal heat, either directly using steam or hot water from underground reservoirs or through ground-source heat pumps that utilize stable subsurface temperatures for heating and cooling. Energy storage technologies are increasingly vital for managing renewable intermittency. These include batteries (particularly lithium-ion) storing electrical energy through electrochemical reactions; pumped hydro storage using excess electricity to pump water uphill for later release through turbines; and emerging technologies like hydrogen production where electricity splits water molecules to create storable fuel. Microgrid systems integrate multiple renewable sources with storage and smart controls, enabling localized energy management that increases resilience and efficiency while potentially operating independently from larger grids.

scenario.title: Treehouse Power Designer
scenario.content: Students design and manage energy systems for a self-sufficient treehouse, integrating various renewable technologies to meet changing power needs. The simulation allows students to select, size, and position different energy componentsâsolar panels, wind turbines, micro-hydro generators, biomass systems, and storage solutionsâbased on environmental conditions and structural constraints. The system visualizes energy flows from generation through storage to consumption, displaying real-time power production, usage patterns, and environmental impacts. Students can manipulate variables including weather conditions, seasonal changes, energy demand profiles, and budget constraints to test system resilience. Interactive tools demonstrate scientific principles behind each technology, showing electron flow in photovoltaic cells, aerodynamic effects on wind turbines, and electrochemical processes in batteries. Challenge scenarios require students to optimize systems for different geographic locations, address unexpected equipment failures, or adapt to changing household needs, teaching both technical aspects of renewable energy and practical system design considerations.

hypothesis.description: Students will design renewable energy solutions by analyzing resource availability and consumption patterns. They will evaluate how different generation and storage technologies perform under varying conditions, and create integrated systems that provide reliable, sustainable power with minimal environmental impact.
